In my experience, you do not "keep" a happy marriage. You orbit around a happy marriage, but every couple years, you go into a rough patch. The trick is learning how to get back to the happy side of the rough patch with your marriage still intact. This basically comes down to arguing productively.

You can call it the difference between a "disagreement" and an "argument". Responsible adults should be able to have a discussion about a disagreement without it divulging into a fight. You've married the woman. One hopes that accompanied a certain amount of mutual respect and admiration. So, when you have a disagreement, there ought to be a way to work out some sort of understating or compromise.

So, when you argue (an¬¬¬d you will argue) and when you disagree (and you will disagree), make a concerted effort into being mature about it. For us, the basic rule is that the first person to get mad was the one who blew it. Even if you’re in the midst of a severe disagreement, respectful adults should be able stay cool and approach the disagreement in a responsible way most of the time.

And just to be clear, it's okay to get pissed off from time to time. Nobody’s perfect, but if you get pissed off, you still try to only talk about why you're upset and not just to say hurtful things in retaliation. That’s the key. Some people, when they’re hurt by someone, use words as weapons to hurt the other person back. This is just a terrible terrible habit that has no place in a harmonious marriage. Someone may say a hurtful thing from time to time, but you basically have a pact with your partner that no matter how bad things get, you’re always working towards a solution, not just trying to be mean.

Also, have patience. Marriage lasts a long time. If you’re spending the rest of your life with someone, there’s no reason to freak out if you have a rough path that lasts for a few weeks or even a few months. People will tell you communicate. Think about what that means for a second. Most people will take that as talk about everything. Thaaaaat is not such a great policy. Especially if you consider communicating to be unfiltered. DO NOT DO THAT. I have seen people do that, it generally doesn't end well. You end up saying something stupid, hurting their feelings, it breeds resentment, and before you know it you are heading to a lawyer. If you know your partner well enough, you should know the kind of things you can't say to them, and those that you can.

By communicating generally take into account their feelings. It is no longer just you, and you can't live like it is. Even if you don't like those feelings, consider them to be at all valid, based in reason, or whatever. You still need to consider them. You don't always have to value the opinion someone holds. My wife doesn't always value mine, and I don't always value hers. Both of us are sometimes wrong, and that's a perfectly reasonable reason to disagree, and a reason to consider someone's opinion in that particular matter as not holding much weight. The trick is, thinking someone is wrong, or not valuing their opinion in a circumstance when they are wrong still needs to go through a few steps.

  1. Make damn sure they are actually wrong, or you are actually right. This requires getting outside of your head, and empathizing. Try to figure out where they are coming from. Are they still absolutely wrong? Can you see their point?

  2. Are you right? If you aren't absolutely certain of that after a triplecheck (or possibly using a friend or confidante as a red team), you probably aren't.

  3. Most importantly. Not valuing someone's opinion in a situation where they are wrong, or disagreeing with them on a matter of opinion, does not mean you do not value them. Never lose sight of that. Ever.
